title: How much of a nervous-system model does behaviour identify? Code, results and reproduction container
description:
Code, result files and a one-command reproduction container for a study measuring how much of a whole-organism nervous-system model behaviour actually constrains. A single Gauss-Newton curvature estimator is applied to every system, and each reported dimension is accompanied by the checks that make it meaningful: whether the observables outnumber the parameters, whether the response is proportional to the perturbation, and what the simulator's own noise floor is.

Main findings. In the connectome-scale nematode model (3076 synaptic and gap-junction weights) behaviour constrains 8 directions at 90% of the curvature and 47 at 99%; a connectome-constrained Drosophila optic-lobe model gives 14 of 330, so in two phyla behaviour reaches a few per cent of a connectome-scale parameter space. The low dimension is a property of the region rather than of one parameter point, and does not depend on which layer of the model is read. Chemical synapses carry 87% of the curvature and gap junctions 13%; the conductances behaviour leaves free are the fast voltage-gated calcium currents. Further aspects of one action re-measure the combinations that action already determines and the union saturates, whereas an action with a different functional demand determines directions the first cannot reach. Where the true parameters are known, in eleven cell models, a fit can match behaviour to 1e-3 while the parameters remain 40% from the truth, so a perfect behavioural fit does not imply recovered parameters; effective dimension is shown not to be the same quantity as recoverable dimension. The same low-dimensional stiff and sloppy structure appears in four biological datasets that use none of the simulators.

The deposit contains the manuscript and Supplementary Information, every result file underlying the reported quantities, the analysis and figure code, the input data, and a container that re-derives all reported numbers and regenerates the figures.
